text: It's genuinely easy to serve a model badly: load the weights at import time, write a Flask route that calls model dot predict, return JSON, and call it done. That survives a demo. In production it falls apart fast, because none of the real problems are handled — concurrent requests hitting one process serially, no safe way to roll out a new model version, and every model reimplementing the same plumbing from scratch.

A real serving framework solves four concrete problems generically. Model lifecycle: load each model once, keep it warm in GPU memory, version it so you can roll forward or back without dropping requests. Request batching: implement dynamic batching as a configuration option instead of you hand-timing windows yourself. Multi-model serving: host many models, even many versions, on shared infrastructure instead of one pod per model. And a standard protocol, so the rest of your platform doesn't need model-specific glue code.

The real tools split cleanly. NVIDIA Triton Inference Server is a multi-framework runtime — TensorRT, PyTorch, ONNX Runtime, Python backends — with dynamic batching and multi-model hosting built in; it's often the process actually running inside the pod. TorchServe and TensorFlow Serving do the same job for one framework specifically. vLLM is purpose-built for large language models, using continuous batching and PagedAttention to push far higher throughput than a generic framework manages for that workload.

KServe doesn't replace any of those — it sits above them on Kubernetes, built on Knative and Istio, adding the InferenceService custom resource, a standardized V2 inference protocol, scale-to-zero autoscaling, and canary rollouts between model versions. A minimal InferenceService spec names a storage URI and a predictor, like Triton, and notably contains no Deployment, Service, Ingress, or HPA — KServe generates every one of those underneath on your behalf.

So the layering is: a predictor like Triton or TorchServe does the actual batched GPU inference, and a Kubernetes-native layer like KServe or Seldon Core standardizes and automates everything around it. Knowing these names and what each one actually owns is what lets you read a real production inference stack instead of guessing. Next lesson turns to the cost side — why naive autoscaling of GPU-backed pods wastes money fast, and what the real patterns look like instead.
